title: JavaScript Collections: Map, Set, and WeakMap
description: Choose collections by key semantics, uniqueness, ordering, and data lifetime.
learningOutcomes: Explain Map key identity and insertion ordering.
Use Set for unique primitive values and recognize its limits for objects.
Choose WeakMap/WeakSet for object-associated metadata and account for non-enumerability.
Aggregate domain data without mutating inputs.
Use Map methods/iteration, perform basic Set operations, and explain symbol-key visibility.

blocks.text: JavaScript collections: Map, Set, and weak references

Map and Set are specialized collections, not array methods. Map stores key–value pairs and accepts keys of any type; Set stores unique values. WeakMap and WeakSet suit metadata whose lifetime should follow an object key. Choose a structure for its operations and data semantics—not on an assumption that it is automatically faster.

steps.title: Use an object as a key
steps.explanation: Map accepts keys of any type. Here the object key associates state with this exact card object rather than with a string.

steps.title: Setting an existing key updates it
steps.explanation: A Map has one entry per key. Calling set again with the same object does not create a second entry.

steps.title: Inspect lookup, size, and order
steps.explanation: The results are ready, size 2, and keys in their first-insertion order. A new object { id: "a" } is not the same key: objects compare by identity.

blocks.text: Use Map methods and iteration deliberately

steps.title: Initialize a Map
steps.explanation: Map accepts keys of different types and retains insertion order. It is initialized here from entry pairs so the starting data is explicit.

steps.title: Use Map's common methods
steps.explanation: `has` checks membership independently of the value; `get` may return `undefined` for a missing key. `set` inserts/replaces, `delete` removes an entry, and `size` reports the number of entries.

steps.title: Iterate through keys and values
steps.explanation: A Map iterates as `[key, value]` pairs. `keys()` and `values()` expose iterators for the corresponding sequence; `forEach` is another option.

blocks.text: Use `has` when you must distinguish a missing key from a key mapped to `undefined`. Map supports insertion-ordered iteration, and object keys use reference identity.

blocks.text: Set: unique values, not deep object equality

steps.title: Create a set
steps.explanation: The duplicate string collapses: Set uses SameValueZero semantics for primitive values.

steps.title: Adding the same value is idempotent
steps.explanation: The repeated review value changes nothing; the new done string is appended in insertion order.

steps.title: Account for object identity
steps.explanation: has returns true. The last Set has size 2: the two object literals are different references even though their fields match.

steps.title: Build the input sets
steps.explanation: Each Set keeps one copy of a value under JavaScript equality semantics. Separate objects with identical fields remain distinct values because objects compare by identity.

steps.title: Combine their values
steps.explanation: Union combines both sets without repeated values. The example constructs a new Set rather than mutating either original.

steps.title: Compare shared and distinct values
steps.explanation: Intersection keeps values in the first set that are present in the second; difference keeps values from the first that are absent. Order follows iteration of the first set.

blocks.title: Set does not deduplicate by domain key
blocks.text: Set removes duplicate values according to JavaScript equality semantics, but it does not merge separate objects with the same id. To deduplicate records by id, normalize through a Map/Set of ids or define an explicit normalization rule.

steps.title: Associate private metadata with an object
steps.explanation: A WeakMap does not enumerate keys and does not keep an object key alive solely because of the collection entry. While dialog is reachable by the program, its metadata can be read.

steps.title: Check the API's limits
steps.explanation: WeakMap has neither size nor an iterator: observation must not depend on nondeterministic garbage collection. The final line throws TypeError because WeakMap is not iterable. The final line tries to iterate WeakMap and intentionally throws TypeError.

blocks.text: WeakSet similarly tracks object membership, such as DOM nodes already processed. “Weak” does not mean a cleanup timer or a cache with an observable size: garbage-collection timing is nondeterministic. If you need iteration, counting, or guaranteed deletion, use ordinary Map/Set and manage lifetime explicitly.
Symbols: unique keys and well-known protocols

steps.title: Compare local and registry symbols
steps.explanation: A new `Symbol('id')` is unique even if another symbol has the same description. `Symbol.for('app.id')` uses the global registry and returns the same symbol for the same registry key.

steps.title: Inspect symbol-keyed properties
steps.explanation: `Object.keys` returns enumerable own string-keyed properties, so it omits symbol-keyed properties. `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` can retrieve them.

steps.title: Use the iterable protocol
steps.explanation: `Symbol.iterator` is the protocol used by `for...of` and spread. This object delegates iteration to its contained array.

blocks.title: Symbols are not private storage
blocks.text: Symbol keys can reduce accidental name collisions, but they do not make data secret. Code can inspect them with `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` or `Reflect.ownKeys`; they are not a security boundary.

blocks.prompt: A record has a symbol-keyed own property. What does `Object.keys(record)` return?

options.text: Only enumerable own string-keyed property names; symbol keys are omitted
options.feedback: Object.keys returns enumerable string-keyed own property names. Use Object.getOwnPropertySymbols or Reflect.ownKeys to inspect symbol keys.

options.text: All own keys, including symbols and non-enumerable properties
options.feedback: Reflect.ownKeys returns all own string and symbol keys, including non-enumerable ones.

options.text: No keys, because a symbol makes the entire record private
options.feedback: A symbol does not make an object or its properties private; symbol-keyed properties remain inspectable.
Object.keys does not enumerate inherited properties.

blocks.explanation: Symbol keys are omitted by Object.keys because it returns enumerable own string-keyed properties. Symbol keys are discoverable through reflection APIs and are not a security mechanism.

blocks.title: Group cart lines by product
blocks.context: A cart receives repeated product lines. Sum quantities by stable productId, preserve the first-seen order, and separately collect unique categories.

blocks.prompt: Which requirement is a good reason to choose WeakMap instead of Map?

options.text: Keys must be enumerable so the UI can show size and every entry.
options.feedback: WeakMap is intentionally not iterable and has no size; use Map for an observable collection.

options.text: Metadata should be retrieved by an object without keeping that object alive solely through the collection.
options.feedback: Correct. WeakMap fits object-associated metadata when enumeration is unnecessary.

options.text: Keys must include arbitrary strings and numbers.
options.feedback: WeakMap keys are objects, not arbitrary primitives.

options.text: The entry must be removed exactly one minute later.
options.feedback: Weak references do not define a cleanup deadline; garbage collection is nondeterministic.

blocks.explanation: WeakMap associates values with object keys without making an object reachable solely through the entry. The trade-off is no enumeration or size, and the application cannot control when memory is reclaimed.

items: Map: key–value pairs with any key type and insertion order; object keys compare by reference identity.
Set: unique values by JavaScript equality semantics; separate objects with equal fields remain distinct.
WeakMap/WeakSet: non-enumerable collections with object keys/elements and weak reachability.
Collection choice determines available operations and semantics; measure performance instead of assuming it.
